# Read/Write Sets & Conflict Analysis

## 1. Transaction Read/Write Sets

| Txn | Read Set RS(Ti) | Write Set WS(Ti) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | {A, B} | {A, B} | Read–modify–write on both items |
| T2 | {A, B} | {A, B} | Read–modify–write on both items |
| T3 | {A, B} | **∅** | Read-only |

## 2. Potential Conflicts (by set intersection)

Since the history fixes only per-transaction order (all three run concurrently), direction is resolved at runtime. Set-intersection tests show what *can* materialize:

| Pair | RS(Ti) ∩ WS(Tj) → rw | WS(Ti) ∩ RS(Tj) → wr | WS(Ti) ∩ WS(Tj) → ww |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 ↔ T2 | {A, B} ✓ | {A, B} ✓ | {A, B} ✓ |
| T1 ↔ T3 | {A, B} ✓ | {A, B} ✓ | ∅ ✗ |
| T2 ↔ T3 | {A, B} ✓ | {A, B} ✓ | ∅ ✗ |

**Every pair conflicts on both A and B.** T3, being read-only, can never produce a ww edge, and per item exactly **one** of wr/rw materializes (T3 reads exactly one version of each).

## 3. Full Conflict Enumeration (pair × item × type)

**T1 ↔ T2** (both RMW the same items — all three types, direction per interleaving):

| Item | rw (Rᵢ < Wⱼ) | wr (Wᵢ < Rⱼ) | ww (Wᵢ < Wⱼ) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | T1→T2 *or* T2→T1 | T1→T2 *or* T2→T1 | T1→T2 *or* T2→T1 |
| B | T1→T2 *or* T2→T1 | T1→T2 *or* T2→T1 | T1→T2 *or* T2→T1 |

**T1 ↔ T3** and **T2 ↔ T3** (writer vs read-only — wr or rw only, mutually exclusive per item):

| Pair | wr | rw |
|---|---|---|
| T1 → T3 | W1(A) < R3(A): T3 reads from T1's version | R3(A) < W1(A): T1 overwrites after T3's snapshot |
| T2 → T3 | W2(A) < R3(A): same, for T2 | R3(A) < W2(A): same, for T2 |
| (item B) | identical shape | identical shape |

## 4. Concrete Instantiation (canonical interleaving)

One legal global order — T2's reads land early, T1 commits first, T3 snapshots after both:

```
R2(A)₀, R2(B)₀, R1(A)₀, W1(A)₁, R1(B)₀, W1(B)₁, C1,
W2(A)₂, W2(B)₂, C2, R3(A)₂, R3(B)₂, C3
```

| # | Ops | Type | Edge | Item |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | R2(A) < W1(A) | **rw** | T2 → T1 | A |
| 2 | R2(B) < W1(B) | **rw** | T2 → T1 | B |
| 3 | R1(A) < W2(A) | **rw** | T1 → T2 | A |
| 4 | R1(B) < W2(B) | **rw** | T1 → T2 | B |
| 5 | W1(A) < W2(A) | **ww** | T1 → T2 | A |
| 6 | W1(B) < W2(B) | **ww** | T1 → T2 | B |
| 7 | W2(A) < R3(A) | **wr** | T2 → T3 | A |
| 8 | W2(B) < R3(B) | **wr** | T2 → T3 | B |

(T1–T3 has **zero** conflicts in this instance: T3 reads T2's versions, not T1's. A different interleaving would shift reads-from to T1→T3 and flip directions.)

## 5. Observations

- **T1–T2 is the dangerous pair:** bidirectional rw edges (#1,#3 and #2,#4) close a cycle with the ww edges (#5,#6) → **G-single**, the lost-update signature. No interleaving of two concurrent RMW writers on the same items can avoid a directed cycle.
- **T3 is cycle-safe:** its edges are all read-side (wr/rw) and cannot participate in a ww pairing; it contributes no path that closes a loop by itself.
- **Under first-committer-wins (SI):** conflict #5/#6 cannot both survive — T2 fails validation at commit, and with it edges #1–#4 and #7–#8 are re-evaluated against T1-only history (T3 then reads from T1 instead: wr T1→T3). Only the abort of one writer makes the conflict set acyclic.
